Voltage is the entire decision, and most buying guides skip it. Most hair dryers sold in Canada are 120V only, and plugging one into a European 220–240V outlet will damage it — sometimes immediately. A plug adapter changes the shape of the plug, not the voltage, so it cannot solve the problem. Voltage was the single most-discussed topic in our entire review dataset at 785 mentions — ahead of noise, weight and price Review analysis. That tells you it is the most common expensive mistake in this category. Our pick: the Dreame Pocket Pro at about C$160, which is dual voltage and carries the joint-highest rating above C$120 in our dataset at 4.6★. If you want the longest-established option, the Dyson Supersonic Travel at about C$400 uses universal voltage.

The short answer on voltage

SituationWhat you needWhat happens if you get it wrong
Using a dryer at home in Canada120V, ALCI plug — standard—
Europe, UK, Australia (220–240V)Dual voltage 110–220V + plug adapterA 120V dryer is damaged, sometimes immediately
United StatesNothing — same 120V, same plug—
Japan (100V)Dual voltage, and expect reduced powerUnderperformance rather than damage
Cruise shipsCheck the line voltage; many are 110VVaries by ship

Three terms to read carefully on a listing:

  • “Dual voltage” — runs on both 120V and 220–240V. Some switch automatically, some have a manual selector
  • “Universal voltage” — same practical meaning, used by Dyson
  • “Compact” or “travel size” — only describes size. It does not mean dual voltage

That third one is where buyers get caught. In our dataset, several listings use “compact” and “travel” interchangeably without stating a voltage range. If a listing does not state dual or universal voltage explicitly, assume it is 120V only.

What a plug adapter cannot fix

This is the single most expensive misunderstanding in this category, so it is worth stating precisely.

A plug adapter changes the physical shape of the connection. It lets a North American plug fit a European socket. It does nothing to the electricity.

A voltage converter changes the electricity. It steps 220–240V down to 120V, or up. Hair dryers draw high wattage — often 1,600W to 1,875W — so a converter has to be rated comfortably above that. Cheap travel converters rated at 50W or 100W are intended for phone chargers and will fail, sometimes dangerously, on a hair dryer.

The practical conclusion: buying a dual-voltage dryer is almost always cheaper and safer than buying a converter capable of running a single-voltage dryer. For the price of a suitable converter you can buy the Revlon travel dryer outright.

What about hotel-provided dryers? They exist, and they are usually weak. If you are travelling with curly hair and need a diffuser, a hotel dryer will not have one — which is an argument for the Dreame Pocket Pro, since it includes a diffuser and dual voltage in one unit.

Two safety checks before you travel

Both of these come out of our review data, and both are quick.

1. Check the ALCI plug on arrival at home, not at the airport. ALCI plugs provide shock protection and are the North American standard for hair dryers. One Canadian reviewer flagged a dryer sold on Amazon.ca as non-compliant and recalled because it lacked the mandatory ALCI plug. Look for the rectangular GFCI-style box with test and reset buttons on the plug end.

2. Check the cord strain relief. Cord and connector failure accounted for 417 mentions in our dataset, the second most common failure mode after complete stoppage at 601. A dryer that gets packed and unpacked is more exposed to that stress than one that stays on a shelf. See how long hair dryers actually last.

One thing not to worry about: the dryer’s weight. Size and storage was the most positively discussed topic in our entire dataset at 1,429 mentions and 74% positive — buyers notice when a travel dryer is genuinely packable.

Frequently asked questions

Can I use my Canadian hair dryer in Europe? Only if it is dual voltage. Most Canadian hair dryers are 120V only, and plugging one into a 220–240V outlet will damage it, sometimes immediately. A plug adapter changes the shape of the plug, not the voltage, so it cannot solve this. Voltage was the most-discussed topic in our entire dataset at 785 mentions.

What does dual voltage mean on a hair dryer? It means the dryer can run on both 120V (North America) and 220–240V (Europe, UK, Australia). Some switch automatically and some have a physical selector you must set before plugging in. If a dryer does not state dual voltage or universal voltage on the listing, assume it is 120V only.

Do I need a voltage converter or just an adapter? For a dual-voltage dryer you need only a plug adapter. For a single-voltage dryer you would need a step-up or step-down converter, and hair dryers draw high wattage, so the converter has to be rated well above the dryer’s draw. In practice buying a dual-voltage dryer is cheaper and safer than buying a converter.

What is the best travel hair dryer in Canada? The Dreame Pocket Pro at about C$160 is our pick if you want a high-speed dryer that works abroad, and it is the joint-highest-rated dryer above C$120 in our dataset at 4.6 stars. The Dyson Supersonic Travel at about C$400 uses universal voltage and has the larger review base at 310 Canadian ratings.

Is a compact hair dryer the same as a travel hair dryer? No, and this is where most buyers get caught. Compact refers to size and often a folding handle. Travel usually implies dual voltage. A compact 120V dryer is still unusable in Europe, and in our data several listings use the two terms interchangeably without stating the voltage range.

Will a dual-voltage hair dryer work as well as a full-size one? Usually it is slightly less powerful, because the same motor draws less on 120V than on 240V and manufacturers size the element for both. For travel that is the expected trade. If you mainly dry at home and travel occasionally, the Dreame Pocket Pro is a reasonable compromise; if drying power at home matters most, keep a full-size dryer and buy a cheap travel unit.

Our verdict on travel hair dryers

Confirm the voltage before anything else. If a listing does not say dual or universal voltage explicitly, treat it as 120V only — “compact” and “travel size” describe dimensions, not electricity.

Our pick: the Dreame Pocket Pro at about C$160. Dual voltage, 4.6★, diffuser included, brand-operated listing. It is the one model here that works at home and abroad without compromise on rating.

If you want the safest bet on reliability: the Dyson Supersonic Travel at about C$400. Universal voltage stated plainly, the largest Canadian review base of our picks, and a real service network — at 2× the Dreame.

If you want a cheap second dryer for trips: the Revlon RVDR5034F at about C$19. Roughly 3,106 units a month and BSR #5 make it the volume leader among travel dryers — but verify the voltage yourself, because we could not confirm it from the listing data we hold.

And check the ALCI plug and the cord strain relief on whatever you buy, for the reasons in our guide to how long hair dryers actually last.
